newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ rates break technical levels to close offered.
newsitem.headline: NZ rates break technical levels to close offered.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against yesterday's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (MAR) 92.35 (PREV 92.46) 90-DAYS 7.63 (PREV 7.50)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.20 PCT (PREV 7.20) US 5-YR 6.19 (PREV 6.18)
* NZ debt market ends sharply weaker
* Tech resistance break of 7.55 pct in 90-days prompts slide
* Bonds sold ahead of Greenspan testimony, but spread vs
U.S. Treasuries seen narrowing
New Zealand debt markets were sharply weaker and remained offered at the close on Wednesday after important technical levels were breached in the short end, precipitating a selling flurry.
"Very well offered at the moment," a dealer said of the New
Zealand debt markets in general.

After wages data on Tuesday confirmed the picture of an economy still growing at a reasonable pace, the 90-day bank bill rate rose gradually until it broke through 7.55 percent resistance in early Wednesday trade.
In a market where rates have consistently traded in a 20 point range for the past several weeks, dealers said the technical break may have taken some by surprise.
"I think a few of the players might have been a bit long, expecting it to trade within that range again. A few of them may have stopped-out," said one.
Although sentiment was bearish and the short end looked technically vulnerable, rates were now reaching levels where buying could re-emerge.

"Technically, I think we can see 90-days a few points higher, but from a medium-term point of view I think we're starting to get to buy levels here, unless the currency comes off dramatically," the dealer said.
As rates have climed, the Kiwi dollar has weakened, closing Wednesday about 20 points lower.
"The Kiwi is a bit weak, which is adding fuel to the fire at the moment on the upside for yields," one trader said.
Yields also continued to rise in the bond market, which was nervously awaiting Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before a Senate Committee tonight (1500 GMT).
"We've also seen a little bit of corporate borrowing in the swaps, so that's led on to selling in the bonds," said a dealer.
"But it's starting to get to levels now where it's probably gone a bit too far -- we're starting to see some offshore investing interest."

He said the spread between the New Zealand 10-year bond and its U.S. counterpart was now considerably wider and may narrow depending on how U.S. Treasuries react to Greenspan's statement. "If the U.S. gets bought tonight, our market might get bought further because it's been sold so far, and if the U.S. sells off overnight, maybe our market might not go as far," he said.
